headlineRealityAssessment.headlineOrClaim: OpenAI, Claude, and Gemini's Reasoning Got Cracked.
headlineRealityAssessment.ordinaryReaderTakeaway: My normal private ChatGPT or Claude conversations, passwords and personal information may have been silently posted online.
headlineRealityAssessment.originalEvidence: The August 10 preprint examined complete AI-work files that developers and researchers had deliberately posted publicly on repositories such as GitHub and Hugging Face, then tested whether provider-specific hidden material in those files could be reconstructed.
headlineRealityAssessment.establishes: Some deliberately public complete AI-work files contained sensitive material beyond the visible conversation, and the authors report that certain tested hidden artifacts could be replayed into related models during the study period.
headlineRealityAssessment.doesNotEstablish: It does not establish that ordinary private consumer chats were silently published, that copying a selected answer exposes the complete file or that every provider and current model still behaves as tested.

scopeLimits.population: Public files posted by developers and researchers, not a sample of ordinary private consumer-chat accounts.
scopeLimits.comparison: The study distinguishes material in the visible conversation from material in the complete behind-the-scenes file.
scopeLimits.measurement: A targeted, non-exhaustive preprint scan with an AI-assisted privacy-violation labeler and no independent LAiDIES reproduction.
scopeLimits.date: Preprint dated August 10, 2026; provider behavior is bounded to the tested period and configurations.
scopeLimits.otherLimits: The authors report the disclosed attacks no longer worked, but LAiDIES has not independently verified a current universal fix state.

headlineRealityAssessment.realConsequence: People who publish complete AI-work or diagnostic files may expose more information than the clean visible answer suggests and need a deliberate release-file process.
headlineRealityAssessment.directlyAffected: Developers, researchers and organizations that publish or reuse complete AI-work or diagnostic files; ordinary users are affected only if they are asked to share that kind of complete file.
headlineRealityAssessment.unknowns: Current behavior across every model and provider, the exact origin of every recovered item and universal remediation remain unknown.
headlineRealityAssessment.mismatchReason: The likely every-chat interpretation materially changes reader fear and action. The evidence supports a narrower deliberate-record publication risk, so the article must correct the panic before explaining the mechanism.

readerEntry.immediateCorrection: The study did not find that ordinary private chats were silently posted online; it examined complete behind-the-scenes files that developers and researchers had deliberately uploaded publicly.
readerEntry.actualActor: Developers and researchers chose to publish files created while their AI software completed tasks.

readerEntry.sharingReason: They uploaded the files so other people could inspect, study or reuse how the AI work happened.
readerEntry.directAudience: People and teams who build with AI and publish complete work or diagnostic files.
readerEntry.ordinaryReaderImpact: Readers at every use level can distinguish information given to AI, visible results, an automatically created activity record and the later audience; the paper directly studied only the public activity-record route.
readerEntry.whyLaidiesCovers: LAiDIES is correcting an alarming misread and giving readers one information-flow model that works for phone questions, work documents and project-wide AI tools.

attackMechanism.ordinaryMeaning: A deliberate security test, not an automatic event affecting every AI user.
attackMechanism.testedAction: Researchers moved an unreadable bundle created by a stronger model into a weaker sibling model from the same provider, used instructions designed to bypass safeguards and asked it to reproduce the hidden contents.
attackMechanism.stoppedWorkingMeaning: After disclosure, that exact model-to-model decoding method no longer revealed hidden contents in the authors' tests.
attackMechanism.limit: This does not prove every possible AI privacy problem is fixed.

draftArchitecture.plainAnswer: No: the study did not find that ordinary private AI chats were silently posted online. It found sensitive information in saved AI-run records that developers and researchers had deliberately uploaded publicly.
causalSequence: A developer uses an AI coding tool and the tool saves a machine-readable record of the run.
The record contains visible instructions, answers and tool actions plus an opaque string carried between steps.
The developer deliberately uploads the original record to GitHub or Hugging Face so others can inspect or reproduce the work.
The paper's researchers download public records and, during the test period, use related models to recover some hidden material.
The authors report the evaluated attacks stopped working after disclosure, while the safer publication lesson remains.
draftArchitecture.workedCase: A developer posts the original activity record from an AI coding task so another researcher can reproduce the work; the visible conversation is clean but an opaque field repeats a key the tool was asked to remove.
draftArchitecture.transferCase: A traveller selects only the visible itinerary words from a private AI chat and pastes them into an email; those selected words are not the activity record studied in the paper.
draftArchitecture.usefulAction: Share a fresh allowlisted report or the checked final result, strip reasoning/signature/opaque fields from technical releases and rotate credentials if raw logs touched secrets while public.

evidenceAnalysis.claimUnderInspection: A new study means hidden AI reasoning is currently exposing ordinary users' private chats.
evidenceAnalysis.primaryEvidence: Panfilov et al. preprint plus current OpenAI, Anthropic and Google documentation on opaque reasoning or thought-state fields.
evidenceAnalysis.establishes: The authors reconstructed opaque reasoning data from public technical session records, found real secrets and demonstrated cross-context attacks during the tested period.
evidenceAnalysis.doesNotEstablish: A continuing exploit after disclosure, exposure caused by ordinary private chat use, leakage from every raw log or exact fidelity for every reconstructed token.
evidenceAnalysis.claimedImpact: All hidden AI reasoning is unsafe and users should ask the model to reveal it.
evidenceAnalysis.realConsequence: People who publish raw technical AI sessions must treat opaque fields as unreviewed data and release only approved fields; asking for reasoning is not a security check.
evidenceAnalysis.aidbReason: The exact paper was absent from the scheduled August 12 edition, but LAiDIES inspected representative public AIDB Reality Check analyses on August 15 and used their claim-versus-measurement discipline only as a detection lens. Ali supplied the separate discovery lead; LAiDIES independently read the primary evidence.

representativeProofPlan.highestRisk: Correcting the panic but still leaving the reader unable to name the public paper, the saved record, the complete sharing route or when it applies.
representativeProofPlan.plannedProof: Before technical labels, a cold reader must identify the public paper and claim, explain who created and uploaded which record where and why, distinguish five sharing routes and name one concrete unintended-content example plus the origin uncertainty.
representativeProofPlan.acceptanceOutcome: Without repeating task record, log, trace, session, export or API, the reader can reconstruct the event and say exactly whether it changes anything for her.
